subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL COMMISSION-ALLEGED NOTIFICATION TO MUNICIPALITIES THAT DUMPING ON ITS LANDS WILL BE PROHIBITED IN 1974
NATIONAL CAPITAL COMMISSION-ALLEGED NOTIFICATION TO MUNICIPALITIES THAT DUMPING ON ITS LANDS WILL BE PROHIBITED IN 1974
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 8, 1973, as reported at page 4575 of Hansard, I asked a question of the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Basford) about the growing concern of the people generally in the national capital area with respect to problems affecting waste management disposal in the area. I asked the minister specifically whether the national capital commission had notified the municipalities within the area that dumping on its lands would be prohibited in 1974 and, if so, what was the cut-off date for that order. I am quoting almost exactly, Mr. Speaker. The minister at that time indicated that he would take the matter under advisement.
Subsequently, I had a letter from the general manager of the national capital commission which indicated that there was indeed a problem with respect to the dumping of garbage on national capital commission land, that the land presently being used in this area was being very quickly filled, that by 1974 it would in fact be rendered useless from the point of view of land fill, and that consideration had been given to other methods of disposal.
One of those methods of disposal unfortunately, according to sources that I have, is the acquisition of further dumping ground elsewhere within the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton. Speaking personally, Mr. Speaker, this concerns me greatly because I think it is really a perpetuation of what is generally regarded as self-destroying and a non-modern practice of waste disposal.
July 23, 1973

The national capital commission, however, did indicate to me that they were considering a technical process of waste disposal, one involving incineration, that they had indeed suggested to the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton and perhaps to other municipalities that there was a process available, and that it would be available to the relevant municipalities within the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton. I think this is very important, and not only from the point of view that the national capital must prove itself to be a leader with respect to urban problems, only one of which is waste disposal. The national government ought to give some meat to the attitude that it would like to project in the country, an attitude showing it is interested in urban problems.
I hope the parliamentary secretary's answer tonight will show for the record that the government is considering the technical process of incineration; that the federal government is preparing to finance or fund out of the federal treasury a major proportion, at least, of a pilot project; that the national capital of our country ought to be a leader with respect to municipal services available in this area, and that there will not be any consideration of land acquisition so that municipalities will not need to acquire large tracts of land for 20 years duration, such as is the case with respect to the site south of the Jock River in Nepean township. That, I understand, was one of the considerations brought forward in a consultant's report.
I emphasize to the government through you, Mr. Speaker, that the government should not stop with the national capital area in the funding of programs of this nature. It should as well consider making available this expertise, this technology and, more important, similar funding for these vital municipal services to other large cities across Canada, such as Toronto, Hamilton, Vancouver and Montreal, which are experiencing great difficulties in this area. I hope we shall never see in the national capital area what we are seeing in the metropolitan Toronto area. The garbage and waste from the metropolitan area is being trucked out and deposited in other municipalities. As I said at the outset, this is a self-perpetuating, self-destroying system of waste disposal.
If the answers by the parliamentary secretary to the questions which I have asked in the course of this debate are in the affirmative, I urge the government to give permission to other municipalities to apply for similar funding, so that we may attack on a national basis one of the problems that is affecting municipalities and, particularly, the municipalities within the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Watson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: NATIONAL CAPITAL COMMISSION-ALLEGED NOTIFICATION TO MUNICIPALITIES THAT DUMPING ON ITS LANDS WILL BE PROHIBITED IN 1974
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the NCC has been assisting the city of Ottawa for the past nine years by providing approximately 109 acres of land which is used as a garbage dump and operated as a sanitary land fill site. The ten-year legal agreement for use of this NCC Greenbelt land expires December 31, 1973. The users are fully aware of the expiry date and have been advised that alternate disposal methods must be considered for the future. The capacity of this land fill site is nearly exhausted and another area for sanitary land fill or an alternative means of disposal must soon be found.
Adjournment Debate
Realizing that the problem of waste disposal is of regional concern and that similar problems are being faced by cities and regions across Canada, the NCC, together with MOE, the Municipal Regional Councils of Ottawa-Carleton and Outaouais, have financed a comprehensive study by consultants of waste disposal in the national capital region. The study is to make recommendations for waste disposal with due regard for the protection of the environment. All modern methods of disposal are to be considered, including incineration.
I might add that there are a number of municipalities across the country which would like this type of test facility. The hon. member for Grenville-Carleton (Mr. Baker) makes a good case for the Ottawa region, but he must realize that there are many members from across this country, myself included, who would like to see this kind of test facility installed in their regions, at the expense of the national taxpayer. Ottawa seems to get quite a few of these items. It is woith reminding members from the Ottawa region that there are others in this country who would like a national contribution of this kind in their areas once in a while. In saying that I speak not as the parliamentary secretary but as the member representing Laprairie.
This phasing out may occur sooner than 1975, with the existing sites being covered with soil, landscaped and made into an area suitable for future reforestation. It should be emphasized that the NCC is not prohibiting waste disposal and dumping, but that the agreement will have expired by the end of this year, that the site is full and better solutions have been found for the disposal of waste on a regional basis.
Accordingly, it might be said that there will ultimately be a solid waste disposal system in the regional municipality of Ottawa-Carleton. Recognizing this, the NCC and the Department of the Environment are concentrating their efforts in this regard.

subtopic: HOUSING-ALLEGED POOR CONSTRUCTION OF BAL-MAN HOMES, MEADOW LAKE, SASKATCHEWAN-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
HOUSING-ALLEGED POOR CONSTRUCTION OF BAL-MAN HOMES, MEADOW LAKE, SASKATCHEWAN-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this afternoon I asked the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs (Mr. Watson) whether, in view of the fact that Bal-Man Homes Ltd. built some homes at Meadow Lake, Saskatchewan, of substandard quality, and in view of the fact that this company has not paid some of the subconstractors, this resulting in mechanics liens being registered against the homes, the minister had requested the Saskatoon office of CMHC to conduct a full scale investigation of this matter to ensure that the home buyers are protected. In his wisdom, Mr. Speaker ruled that this question was out of order. Of course, I accepted that. He invited me to participate in the debate tonight which I am doing.
If I had been allowed to ask a supplementary question, it would have been something like this-I hope the parliamentary secretary takes note of it. Is it the policy of Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to require borrowers to pay interest on the full amount of mortgage, in spite of the fact these borrowers have not received the
5910

July 23, 1973
Adjournment Debate
full amount of mortgage money because of a holdback due to improper finishing of a home?
This may sound like a minor problem, but seven householders in one town have complained to me on various occasions. The minister's office has received some letters about this problem, dating back some time. To top it all off, I received a telegram this morning urgently requesting some action on this matter. I feel that action is required.
I spoke to several of these householders over the telephone. I have a rough transcript of what one told me. During 1970-71 and 1972, Bal-Man Homes of Saskatoon built several houses in Meadow Lake. He understands there were several built in other centres, including Biggar, Rosetown and Saskatoon. He said he does not know much about the ones in other centres, but in Meadow Lake it appears the houses are basically structurally sound. However, substandard workmanship did go into the finishing of these houses in many instances. There were things like paint jobs with inadequate sanding, inadequate covering of the material on the gyproc, and so on. Initially, the CMHC inspector passed these homes. He took exception, stating that this was not correct, that the houses had not been painted properly. The inspector came and inspected them and agreed it was not up to standard.
He wrote to Bal-Man Homes and CMHC, but to no avail. Approximately two months after they had moved into their homes they started getting notices from the land titles office in North Battleford that mechanics liens were being placed against the homes by different contractors such as roofers, plumbers, suppliers of materials and so on.
They asked the CMHC lawyer in Meadow Lake what could be done. No one got a satisfactory answer except that it appeared they would have to pay off these liens. They wrote many letters and received a different answer each time. Sometimes they were told they could take legal action against Bal-Man Homes. At other times they were told that Bal-Man Homes was bankrupt, or there was impending receivership and legal action. They were told their statutory declaration was signed to the effect the work was completed and paid for before CMHC approved disbursement of the funds. It seems odd, though, that CMHC did not insist on having receipts as well as a statutory declaration from the contractor. He said they had contacted the manager and assistant manager of CMHC in Saskatoon but had not managed to get any satisfactory answer as to what effect these mechanics liens would have on them. One person was told to forget about them, that they did not mean anything. Others were told that the mechanics liens would stay on indefinitely and collection made either before or at the time of sale.
He said they were paying CMCH the full amount of their mortgage payments, or were until July 1 when he discontinued until he got some satisfaction. He said he notified the minister that he was doing this. He said that CMHC continue to tell them they will have to wait until a trustee is appointed and an investigation conducted, that an investigation is being carried out and that eventually their homes will be fit to live in.
In many cases he said they could not afford to wait. There are three who are subject to immediate transfer by their employers, one to be transferred on August 1. He

must be able to sell his house to some one else with a clear title, except for the CMHC mortgage, in order that he can move and recover his investment. There has just been no action on this at all.
He said they are waiting for the finishing to be done on these homes; they have piles of dirt in the front yards, the shingles on the roofs are not properly fastened down and the venting is not completed properly. He suggested that small things like this will cause the homes to deteriorate and that they have no money right now to fix up what they have already paid for through their mortgages.
I understand the money was loaned directly by CMHC for the purpose of building low-income homes on speculation by Bal-Man Homes Limited. Furthermore I understand that money was held back as homes were not adequately completed, but that the borrowers had to pay interest on the entire principal. I should like to have some comment from the parliamentary secretary on the matters I have raised tonight.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ian Watson (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of State for Urban Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Urban Affairs
subtopic: HOUSING-ALLEGED POOR CONSTRUCTION OF BAL-MAN HOMES, MEADOW LAKE, SASKATCHEWAN-REQUEST FOR INVESTIGATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in replying to the subject matter raised, the 11 units in Meadow Lake are being built under the assisted home-ownership program, the builder having obtained speculative loans under the program. The 11 units have been sold with the majority being occupied by the purchasers who have been making payments on the mortgages.
Final inspections have not yet been made on any of the houses and the corporation has mortgage moneys on hand sufficient to complete the houses should the builder not be in a position to do so. Under these circumstances the purchasers are not in any danger of losing their equity or the money paid on monthly mortgage payments. I am sure the hon. member will be happy to be able to assure his constituents of that fact.
Incidentally, the purchasers would also be eligible for assistance, as I mentioned privately to the hon. member this afternoon, under Section 8.1 of the new legislation, Bill C-133, although there would seem to be no reason to expect in this case such assistance would be necessary as CMHC has withheld funds.
Although purchasers are making full monthly payments on their mortgages, even though all mortgage moneys have not been advanced, they are not in the final analysis being called upon to pay interest on money not advanced-and this the hon. member can report to his constituents as well-because interest credits will subsequently be made to their accounts.
The hon. member will also be interested to learn that the manager and assistant manager of CMHC, the Saskatoon office, are meeting the purchasers in Meadow Lake on the evening of July 24, that is tomorrow night, for the purpose of reviewing the situation and answering the questions of the homeowners. This afternoon I asked CMHC officals to ask their people in the field to exert maximum pressure on the builder and whoever is responsible there to complete these houses, remedy the deficiencies which apparently do exist and try to bring matters up to the satisfaction of the purchasers.
July 23, 1973

Mr. Speaker, my comments tonight arise from a question I asked on Friday last of the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) concerning Information Canada. I asked it in light of the Prime Minister's expressed view that the agency was now regarded as a propaganda machine and it was going to be disbanded. The minister lamentably replied it was not.
I want to cite three particular reasons for disbanding Information Canada. The first is the waste involved, the second is partisan abuse, and the third, the most important, is the view that it is simply an improper power for the government to have at this time.
I want to deal first with waste. When the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) introduced Information Canada during the 1970's, he said:
The object will be to increase effectiveness as well as to save money by reducing duplication in the use of staff and equipment and by better joint use of the government's information resources.
I want to draw attention to two particular phrases; the first "saving money", the second, the idea of "reducing duplication". Since the establishment of Information Canada, nine departments alone have increased their own internal information budgets from $19 million in 1970-71 to fully $36 million in 1972-73, almost a doubling of expenditure. There was a commitment at that time that only 150 individuals would be associated with the on-going activities of Information Canada. Now there are 192. There was a commitment then that there would be only 25 information officers; already there are 38.
What is worse, Sir, is that despite this waste and growth Information Canada is not doing its job. Most members in this House are acquainted with the slowness of the agency. Far more important, the director of regional operations said in May of this year that the program, which is designed to reach out to the 43 per cent of Canadians whom the government considers do not know what is going on in Canada, is not working. One of the reasons it is not working is this; the government is running offices of the kind these people never reach. As a bold new initiative they are sending out a salesman on a bicycle in Nova Scotia to try to acquaint people with the work of Information Canada and to drum up business. That is a complete confession of failure of the agency. Much more stark is the Prime Minister's statement the other day. One other indication of that is that Information Canada, which was presumably created to meet a public need for information, has now had to set up its own public relations bureau to create that need that it was designed to meet.
Mr. R. A. J. Phillips, the former deputy director, in a document which the present director said was "never supposed to be published" said, and I quote: "It is urgent to consider some projects to justify our budget and existence." The upshot of that was that he was moved out of Information Canada to a safer haven. That is a clear example of the outright waste that exists in Information Canada. The greatest effort now is to create a demand for its services and to consider some projects to justify its budget and existence.
Adjournment Debate
I want to make a quick reference to partisan abuse. The first director was a very prominent Quebec Liberal who has now moved out. I think probably that capacity has diminished somewhat, and once the suspicion that there is partisan abuse subsides it will be used for party purposes again.
So beyond the waste and beyond the capacity for partisan abuse, what is really wrong with Information Canada is that it represents a power which it is improper for a government to possess. However it is disguised, it is a means by which the government seeks to impose its particular view of what is right and what is real. It is, to use the Prime Minister's phrase, a "propaganda machine". That is clear whether you accept the official defence that there is a "right to know" among the 43 per cent of Canadians whom the government believes did not know much about what is going on, or whether you need the more frank defence, which members of the government party have expressed to me privately, that the government has to have a better means of reaching Canadians than relying on those guys in the Press Gallery. It is, in short, an attempt to get around the normal filters of democracy; an attempt not to present information, but to manage it.
The failure so far of Information Canada does not make it any less sinister, because the government is determined not to let it fail. That was the clear purport of the statement by the Prime Minister, who proposes to conquer the west by reforming Information Canada, and the response by the Minister of Labour that nothing is wrong with what the government is doing. That betrays the complacent, persisting view that nothing is wrong with what the Liberal government has done; the only fault is in telling. All that is needed is a better propaganda machine.
I wish to suggest in passing that if there were a genuine desire to inform Canadians, the government would not hide so many documents, or avoid so many inquiries, or stamp "secret" on so much public business.
Information Canada must be seen as part of the overweighted capacity of the government to influence opinion and restrict options in Canada. It is a clear example of adding power to the powerful. The native people of James Bay have no Information Canada, nor does the small businessman quietly going broke, nor the legions of the unemployed, nor the old. The weak have no weapon. Even the parties in opposition in Parliament have no Information Canada, no powerful means to present an alternate view. Indeed, while the rules of Parliament have been changed to weaken the opposition, Information Canada has been created to strengthen the government.
That is the context in which the idea of Information Canada is truly alarming. It is a terrible waste when it does not work, as it does not work now. But if the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) ever upgrades it, if he ever succeeds in creating the kind of propaganda machine he wants, there will be less freedom of opinion, less examination of options that we need to survive as a modern democracy.
This question should not end here. I hope the government will have sufficient honesty to refer to the parliamentary committee the whole question of the imbalance of power to influence opinion and express opinion in Canada,

July 23, 1973
Adjournment Debate
instead of staying with Information Canada which is designed to make that imbalance worse.

speakeroldname: Mr. Charles Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Labour):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Information Canada activities related to the reinforcing of the federal presence are as follows. Federal inquiry centres and bookstores have been established by Information Canada in prominent locations in Canadian cities, namely, Montreal, Ottawa, Halifax, Winnipeg and Vancouver. Each is clearly marked with the bar and leaf federal symbol. Some 500,000 inquiries were received last year and the rate is increasing some 20 per cent a year.
Plans for the current year call for the opening of federal inquiry services in the hon. member's province of Alberta, in Saskatchewan, New Brunswick, Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland. Once in place, it can be expected that many more thousands of citizens will avail themselves of the services offered and thus become more aware of the federal presence in this country.
In both Manitoba and Nova Scotia Information Canada is currently working with the regional offices of other federal departments on a development plan to strengthen and support the relationship between the federal government and the people, and in so doing is, of course, extending the federal presence beyond the urban centres to areas where the need for communication is every bit as pressing. Through the activities of the mobile information offices and federal offices, the presence will become manifest in areas previously rarely reached.
Through the launching of the federal identity program, the largest such corporate identity undertaking in the world, Information Canada has made the bar and leaf symbol the sign of the federal presence from one end of Canada to the other. It is seen everywhere on federal buildings, vehicles, aircraft, uniforms, post boxes and so forth. Over 50 federal departments and agencies incorporate the bar and leaf symbol into their letterheads, press releases, on the cover of their publications, and each time it is seen it is recognized as a manifestation of the federal presence.
Given the opportunity to continue the development of its citizen's inquiry service, which is probably unique in the world, the federal presence will become even more manifest in all corners of this country. But it cannot happen overnight and it cannot happen if the agency is not encouraged in its work.
